bodyMarkdown:
## The idea in plain language

A line chart is a bar chart that has been joined up, and that changes what your eye notices. Bars invite you to compare heights; lines invite you to notice **direction** — rising, falling, flattening, crossing.

So line-chart questions lean towards trends and turning points rather than single readings.

## What is actually going on

The steepness of a segment is the rate of change, not the value. A line can be high but falling, or low but climbing fast — and questions deliberately exploit that difference.

When two lines cross, the quantities are equal at that moment; before and after, one leads. Questions about 'in how many years did A exceed B' are answered by reading which line sits on top, interval by interval.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Two colleges' enrolments over 2019-2023 are 820, 865, 790, 910, 960 and 700, 745, 810, 845, 880. In how many years did the second exceed the first?
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Compare year by year:

2019: 700 against 820, no. 2020: 745 against 865, no. 2021: 810 against 790, **yes**. 2022: 845 against 910, no. 2023: 880 against 960, no.

So in exactly 1 year.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: On the chart this is simply the interval where the second line pokes above the first.

formulaCards.title: Reading a line chart
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: Height is the value; steepness is the rate of change; a crossing point means the two values are equal.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: A steeply falling line from 900 to 700 still sits above a flat line at 400.

commonTraps: Confusing the steepest rise with the highest value.
Assuming values between marked points are meaningful. Only the plotted points are data.
Missing a crossing that happens between two labelled years.
